name: Synthetic User Testing
definition: Synthetic user testing uses AI-generated personas, responses, or simulated interactions to explore how people might react to a product. Its outputs are model-generated predictions that require validation against evidence from real users.
sources: Nielsen Norman Group: Synthetic Users vs. Human Respondents (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users-vs-human-respondents/)
contentMarkdown:
# Synthetic User Testing

Synthetic user testing uses AI-generated personas, responses, or simulated interactions to explore how people might react to a product. Its outputs are model-generated predictions that require validation against evidence from real users.

The label covers different activities. An AI persona answering interview questions produces simulated opinions. An agent attempting a task in an interface produces evidence about that agent's performance. Neither directly establishes how representative people will behave.

## Where it can help

A team can use simulations to rehearse interview questions, generate possible objections, or identify scenarios to include in a usability study. These are useful inputs to research planning.

For example, a designer could ask a model to review a booking cancellation flow from several stated perspectives. If it flags a missing refund explanation, the team can inspect the policy and add that topic to its research plan.

A synthetic response that says “I would subscribe” does not establish demand or willingness to pay.

## Limits to check

Generated responses can reflect the assumptions in the prompt, repeat common patterns, and miss unusual behavior. In one NN/g comparison of a terminology survey, synthetic respondents reached a similar overall conclusion but produced less varied answers. That result applies to the study's task and setup; it does not establish general equivalence.

Label simulated findings, record the model and prompts, and keep them separate from participant evidence. Validate important decisions through suitable methods, such as interviews, observed task performance, or behavioral experiments.

Treat disagreement between simulated and observed results as a reason to investigate the assumptions.

name: Autonomous Workflow Orchestration
definition: Autonomous workflow orchestration coordinates tasks, decisions, dependencies, and execution state so an automated system can pursue a goal with limited ongoing supervision. In AI applications, it can combine predefined workflow steps with agent-selected actions.
contentMarkdown:
# Autonomous Workflow Orchestration

Autonomous workflow orchestration coordinates tasks, decisions, dependencies, and execution state so an automated system can pursue a goal with limited ongoing supervision. In AI applications, it can combine predefined workflow steps with agent-selected actions.

“Autonomous” describes the scope of delegated work. The system still needs rules for permissions, stopping, exceptions, and human involvement.

## Example: supplier onboarding

A supplier-onboarding workflow could collect submitted documents, check required fields, request missing information, and prepare a record for approval.

Some checks can run independently. Creating the active supplier account depends on the required checks and approval being complete. If an external verification service is unavailable, the workflow should preserve its state and show what is waiting.

An agent might help interpret an unfamiliar document while the application controls the approval requirement and account-creation operation.

## What orchestration manages

- Dependencies: which steps must finish before another can start.
- State: the inputs, completed work, and pending decisions.
- Recovery: how failures, timeouts, and interruptions are handled.
- Coordination: handoffs between services, agents, and people.
- Limits: when a run must stop or request intervention.

A single agent can participate in an orchestrated workflow; multiple agents are optional.

## Check before retrying

A timeout does not establish that an external operation failed. If account creation returns no result, check the target system before repeating it. Use operation identifiers or idempotency mechanisms where supported.

Test partial completion and resumed runs. Persisting workflow state helps recovery, but external side effects still require deliberate duplicate prevention and reconciliation.

name: Evaluation Harness (AI Evals)
definition: An evaluation harness is the infrastructure that runs tests for an AI system, records what happened, applies scoring criteria, and aggregates results. Teams use it to compare versions and detect changes in behavior.
sources: Anthropic: Demystifying Evals for AI Agents (https://www.anthropic.com/research/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)
contentMarkdown:
# Evaluation Harness (AI Evals)

An evaluation harness is the infrastructure that runs tests for an AI system, records what happened, applies scoring criteria, and aggregates results. Teams use it to compare versions and detect changes in behavior.

An evaluation suite is the collection of test cases. The harness executes those cases. An agent harness, by comparison, runs the agent itself; an evaluation can test that runtime and its model together.

## What a useful test includes

A test case needs an input, relevant starting conditions, and explicit success criteria. The harness should capture the outputs and, when relevant, tool calls and changes in the test environment.

Graders can use code, human judgment, or another model. Use a method appropriate to the claim being checked, and calibrate model-based judgments against reviewed examples.

## Example: updating a customer address

An agent is asked to change a test customer's delivery address. A useful evaluation checks that the correct record contains the requested address, unrelated records remain unchanged, and the final message accurately describes the outcome.

The suite should also cover missing address fields, insufficient permissions, and a tool timeout. A successful-sounding reply alone does not prove that the update happened.

## Make comparisons meaningful

Version the cases, prompts, model configuration, tools, and grading rules. Keep initial conditions comparable and run multiple trials when behavior varies.

Report failures by category alongside aggregate scores. Record latency and cost where they matter to the task.

Keep evaluation cases separate from examples used to tune the system. A strong offline score supports a release decision, while production monitoring and user research provide additional evidence about real use.

name: Context Drift
definition: Context drift describes an AI conversation or agent gradually losing track of the user’s goal, relevant facts, or earlier constraints. Teams use the term to discuss behavior over an interaction, especially when history, retrieved material, and tool results accumulate.
sources: Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents, Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
Lost in the Middle, Liu et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
contentMarkdown:
# Context Drift

Context drift describes an AI conversation or agent gradually losing track of the user’s goal, relevant facts, or earlier constraints. Teams use the term to discuss behavior over an interaction, especially when history, retrieved material, and tool results accumulate.

## What does context drift look like?

An assistant may revert to a rejected option, apply a rule to the wrong record, or continue after the goal has changed. Record the specific failure and the information available at that step. A long conversation can expose such problems, while the same symptom can also come from ambiguous instructions, poor retrieval, or an incorrect tool result.

## Example: A booking assistant forgets a constraint

A traveler asks for a refundable flight arriving before noon. After several alternatives and policy lookups, the assistant recommends a cheaper nonrefundable fare. The team checks whether the refundability requirement remained in the model’s context and whether the tool result described that fare correctly.

A useful task state records the selected traveler, dates, constraints, and unresolved questions. Refresh it when the user changes a requirement. When summarizing history, retain the reason an option was rejected.

## How do you test for drift?

Create a multi-turn task with constraints that remain relevant near the end. Check the final recommendation and intermediate actions against those constraints. Compare context-management changes on the same cases, including a changed requirement and conflicting evidence. Summarization and selective retrieval are approaches to evaluate. Measure whether they preserve the facts the task requires.

## Related terms

- [Context Engineering](/glossary/context-engineering.html)

name: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS)
definition: A multi-agent system (MAS) is a system in which multiple autonomous agents interact to pursue goals in a shared environment. Agents may cooperate, negotiate, or compete. In applications built with language models, agents often divide a task and exchange findings through messages or shared state.
sources: An Introduction to MultiAgent Systems, Michael Wooldridge (https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/michael.wooldridge/pubs/imas/IMAS2e.html)
How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System, Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/research/multi-agent-research-system)
contentMarkdown:
# Multi-Agent Systems (MAS)

A multi-agent system (MAS) is a system in which multiple autonomous agents interact to pursue goals in a shared environment. Agents may cooperate, negotiate, or compete. In applications built with language models, agents often divide a task and exchange findings through messages or shared state.

## How do multi-agent systems work?

Each agent has a goal, information it can access, and actions it can take. The system defines how agents communicate, assign work, resolve disagreements, and decide when to stop. An AI application may use one coordinator to delegate tasks to specialists, or let agents hand work to each other as the task develops.

The agents can use different instructions and tools while sharing the same underlying model. Context engineering determines what each agent receives and what information survives a handoff.

## Example: Researching a travel policy

A coordinator receives a request to compare two travel policies. It assigns each policy to a separate research agent and asks for the relevant passages, their sources, and any gaps. The coordinator combines the findings into a comparison and flags unresolved differences for the user.

This structure is useful when the searches can proceed independently and the findings can be combined. Define which agent owns the final answer and what counts as enough evidence. If one agent fails, the coordinator should identify the missing result before presenting the comparison.

## When should you use multiple agents?

Consider them when a task has separable research directions or needs specialist tools and context. Compare the design with a single-agent baseline on the same tasks. Measure the correctness and completeness of the final result, source quality, task completion, latency, and cost. Inspect handoffs for duplicated work or lost information.

Anthropic’s research system is one published example of an orchestrator coordinating parallel research agents. Its account describes the coordination, evaluation, and operational work involved.
